metadata.title: What Does a Feature-Risk-Assessment Actually Tell You?
metadata.topic: FEATURE RISK ASSESSMENT · WORKING WITH CLAUDE
metadata.purpose: Answer whether asking Claude to run a feature-risk-assessment gets you a safe/not-safe verdict or a documented checklist. Lands the carry-out that the assessment tells you what to look at, not whether it's safe.

beats.narration_text: Someone asks Claude to approve a new feature — clean yes-or-no. Wrong verb. Claude doesn't approve; it assesses — against the same fixed checklist every time. Liam, in for Bear — take it from here.

shot.new_visual_element: Writer types 'Claude, will you approve this new feature?', hesitates on 'approve', corrects to 'assess', lands the real question

beats.narration_text: The tempting move is eyeballing a feature and calling it safe. Take one that looks harmless — users upload a photo ID to prove their age. It's optional, nobody's forced, the quick look stamps it LOOKS FINE. Now watch what that stamp doesn't do. It never asks where the photo lands, how long it stays there, or who can see it once it's in. They optimized the quick look for speed at the expense of coverage — and coverage is where the risk actually lives.

shot.new_visual_element: A feature card gets stamped LOOKS FINE, then three unasked questions land underneath it one at a time

production_viz.label: A quick look, then the questions it skipped
production_viz.mechanic: A feature card reading 'PHOTO ID UPLOAD — AGE VERIFICATION' appears. A quick stamp 'LOOKS FINE' lands on it. Then, one at a time below the card, three questions fade in: 'WHERE DOES IT GO?' / 'HOW LONG IS IT KEPT?' / 'WHO CAN SEE IT?' — the card's border flashes accent as each lands, since the quick look never asked any of them.

beats.narration_text: Here's the actual machinery. One file — SKILL.md — the whole instruction set, plain language. You read it, then work through it one step at a time, in order; no branching unless a step tells you to. What comes out is the same four boxes for every feature: what data's collected, where it's stored, how long it's kept, who can access it. They optimized for uniform structure over expressive detail — a missing box is visible in a glance. Watch the anchor. The photo-ID card, four boxes. What's collected and where — filled. How long, who — still blank. Nothing has been judged yet. Documented, one box at a time.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR — the photo-ID card with four checklist boxes, two filled, two blank

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR — four boxes, two blank
production_viz.mechanic: A one-file SKILL.md chip appears, then a short arrow chain: READ -> STEP BY STEP -> RETURN. It fades. THE ANCHOR. The photo-ID card returns, now with four small boxes arranged around it, labelled WHAT / WHERE / HOW LONG / WHO. WHAT and WHERE fill in ('a photo ID', 'stored on a server'); HOW LONG and WHO stay empty dashes. THIS EXACT CARD AND BOXES RETURN, COMPLETED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: Fill the last two: kept ninety days, visible to support staff. Four boxes complete — and here's where the trade-off shows up in both directions. Filled in is not the same as safe. Documenting where the photo goes doesn't clear the feature; it only makes the answer legible. And the reverse: one flag raised — say the retention window wasn't stated — doesn't kill it either. Here's what's actually happening. They optimized the assessment for visibility, not judgment. It hands whoever decides the four things they need to look at. What to do about them is still on that person.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — all four boxes filled, then splits into 'all filled is not safe' and 'one flag is not killed'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS — filled, then split
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 CARD RETURNS, identical placement, its two blank boxes filling in ('90 days', 'support staff'). All four boxes now read complete. It shrinks and moves up; then splits into two cards below: left reads 'all 4 boxes filled' with a struck-through 'SAFE' beneath it labelled 'documented is not judged safe'; right reads 'one flag raised' with a checkmark 'still a call to make' beneath it labelled 'flagged is not killed'.

beats.narration_text: A feature-risk-assessment doesn't tell you a feature is safe. It tells you what to look at before someone decides.

props.quote: A feature-risk-assessment doesn't tell you a feature is safe. It tells you what to look at before someone decides.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I'm about to sign off on a new user-facing feature and I want to run a feature-risk-assessment on it before anyone calls it safe. Take one specific example — users uploading a photo ID for age verification — and fill in the four assessment fields for it: what data is collected, where it's stored, how long it's kept, and who can access it. For each field, name the defensible default and one concrete way it could go wrong. Then flag which of the four is most likely to be answered dishonestly by a rushed product team. Go deeper: take the flagged field and give me the three questions I should ask the feature owner to close it — and what a bad answer to each one would look like.
